items.stem:
Case study context: Kente Market, an online craft marketplace in Accra, stores products as JSON documents, ranks listings with a neural network and processes orders through a queue-based service.
(a) With the help of a specific example, explain why DROP TABLE should be used with great care in a live database. Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [3]
(b) Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Database structure changes (ALTER TABLE) should be made directly on the live database whenever a new requirement appears." Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) It removes the table definition and every row immediately and usually cannot be undone without a backup; other tables' foreign keys and applications that use the table will also break. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (b) Schema changes should be scripted, tested on a copy, version-controlled and applied in a planned window; direct live changes are only acceptable for trivial, reversible cases.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "data definition language (DDL)"?
options: The part of SQL used to define and change the structure of a database, using CREATE, ALTER and DROP
A separate data structure (often a B-tree) that lets the DBMS find rows by a column value without scanning the whole table
A join that returns every row of the left table, with NULLs where there is no matching row in the right table
The DDL statement that changes an existing table, for example adding, dropping or renaming a column or constraint
items.answer: The part of SQL used to define and change the structure of a database, using CREATE, ALTER and DROP
items.markingKey: A. "data definition language (DDL)" is the part of SQL used to define and change the structure of a database, using CREATE, ALTER and DROP.

items.stem: Explain why constraints are defined in the CREATE TABLE statement rather than checked later by programs.
items.answer: The DBMS then enforces them automatically for every insert or update from any application, guaranteeing integrity centrally and documenting the rules in the schema.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Using ON DELETE CASCADE on all foreign keys makes a database easier and safer to manage.
items.answer: Cascade only where child rows have no meaning without the parent (e.g. order lines); use RESTRICT or soft deletes for important records.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no orphan rows; simpler application code. Arguments against: one accidental delete can wipe large amounts of related data (e.g. all orders of a customer); historical/financial records may need to be kept by law; hides mistakes that RESTRICT would catch. Supported judgement: Cascade only where child rows have no meaning without the parent (e.g. order lines); use RESTRICT or soft deletes for important records.

(one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (c) [2 marks] Columns: VolunteerID, Email2, BirthDate, Hours. ADD COLUMN appends at the end; DROP removes; RENAME keeps the position. 1 mark per correctly applied statement.

items.stem: A student claims that SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the table. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows only from the query result; the stored table is unchanged.
items.markingKey: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows only from the query result; the stored table is unchanged. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:

Write one SQL statement to move every product with Category Garden and Price of at least 8 into Category 'Archive', and state how many rows it affects.

items.stem: "A view stores a copy of the data, so it must be refreshed after the base table changes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A standard view stores only the query and is re-evaluated each time, so it always reflects current data (only materialised views store copies).
items.markingKey: A standard view stores only the query and is re-evaluated each time, so it always reflects current data (only materialised views store copies). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Case study context: Kente Market, an online craft marketplace in Accra, stores products as JSON documents, ranks listings with a neural network and processes orders through a queue-based service.
(a) Ana writes: "ALTER TABLE is used to change the value stored in a field." Explain why this is inaccurate. Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [3]
(b) Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Database structure changes (ALTER TABLE) should be made directly on the live database whenever a new requirement appears. Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) ALTER TABLE changes structure; values are changed with UPDATE. (b) Schema changes should be scripted, tested on a copy, version-controlled and applied in a planned window; direct live changes are only acceptable for trivial, reversible cases.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] ALTER TABLE changes structure; values are changed with UPDATE. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (b) [3 marks] Arguments for: quick response to user needs; no separate test environment to maintain. Arguments against: changes can break applications, queries and foreign keys; locks on large tables may stop the service; no rollback plan if data is lost. Supported judgement: Schema changes should be scripted, tested on a copy, version-controlled and applied in a planned window; direct live changes are only acceptable for trivial, reversible cases. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

items.stem:
Case study context: Pacific Ride, a ride-sharing start-up in Lima, matches drivers to passengers using location data, trains models to set prices and builds its back end from reusable classes.
(a) "ORDER BY Score DESC LIMIT 1 and MAX(Score) always give the same output." Explain the flaw in this statement. Refer to Pacific Ride in your answer. [2]
(b) To what extent is it true that Using SQL queries is always better than exporting data to a spreadsheet for analysis? Refer to Pacific Ride in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) MAX(Score) returns only the highest value (one column); ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 returns a whole row and, with ties, only one of the tied rows. (b) For repeatable or large-scale analysis SQL is superior; spreadsheets suit small, ad-hoc exploration of exported summaries.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] MAX(Score) returns only the highest value (one column); ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 returns a whole row and, with ties, only one of the tied rows. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: SQL works on the live, consistent data and scales to millions of rows; queries can be saved, repeated and secured. Arguments against: spreadsheets are easier for non-specialists and good for charts; one-off small analyses may be faster in a spreadsheet. Supported judgement: For repeatable or large-scale analysis SQL is superior; spreadsheets suit small, ad-hoc exploration of exported summaries. items.stem: "Using ON DELETE CASCADE on all foreign keys makes a database easier and safer to manage." Discuss.
items.answer: Cascade only where child rows have no meaning without the parent (e.g. order lines); use RESTRICT or soft deletes for important records.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no orphan rows; simpler application code. Arguments against: one accidental delete can wipe large amounts of related data (e.g. all orders of a customer); historical/financial records may need to be kept by law; hides mistakes that RESTRICT would catch. Supported judgement: Cascade only where child rows have no meaning without the parent (e.g. order lines); use RESTRICT or soft deletes for important records. items.stem:
Case study context: Pacific Ride, a ride-sharing start-up in Lima, matches drivers to passengers using location data, trains models to set prices and builds its back end from reusable classes.
(a) Distinguish between durability and atomicity. Refer to Pacific Ride in your answer. [2]
(b) "Strict ACID compliance should be enforced in every database application." To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to Pacific Ride in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Atomicity means all-or-nothing execution of a transaction; durability means committed results persist even after a failure. (b) Strict ACID is essential where correctness is critical; for high-scale, low-risk data, relaxed consistency can be justified.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Atomicity means all-or-nothing execution of a transaction; durability means committed results persist even after a failure. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: guarantees correctness of concurrent and failed operations; essential for money, bookings and records. Arguments against: locking and logging reduce throughput; distributed systems may need to relax consistency for availability (BASE); analytics or social feeds tolerate slight staleness. Supported judgement: Strict ACID is essential where correctness is critical; for high-scale, low-risk data, relaxed consistency can be justified.
